explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The search is ordered for the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon (Ezra 6:1), but the scroll is found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media (Ezra 6:2). The search points one way and the answer turns up somewhere else. I've hunted for a spatula in my own bakery and found it in the oven mitt drawer, so I feel this one.

Susa is a good guess for a Persian king, friend, but the text doesn't send us there. The scroll is found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media (Ezra 6:2). Darius's search started in the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon (Ezra 6:1). Susa never comes up in this passage.

Nineveh is a famous address, baker, but it's not on this scroll's mailing label. The scroll is found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media (Ezra 6:2). The search itself was ordered for the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon (Ezra 6:1). Three cities were in the running, and Ecbatana takes the prize.

That's it, friend. The memo says, "Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices…" (Ezra 6:3). This house is built for worship, not just to look pretty on a hill. Cyrus put it in writing, and now it's in the memo.

Tribute is what a king collects, baker, and this memo has Cyrus giving instead. It says, "Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices…" (Ezra 6:3). The house is for offering sacrifices to God. Nobody is paying anybody tribute in that line.

Treasures sound fancy, friend, but that's not the word. The memo says, "Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices…" (Ezra 6:3). It's a place for sacrifices. Gold and silver do show up in the memo, but that's a few verses down (Ezra 6:5).

Not quite, baker. The memo says, "The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury." (Ezra 6:4). So the building costs come from the royal treasury, not from the Jews. The size is in the memo too, sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide (Ezra 6:3). Plans and a payment source, all in one memo.

Right, friend. The memo says, "The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury." (Ezra 6:4). The Jews don't pay the building costs themselves. Think of a contractor who hands you the plans and then says the invoice goes to somebody else.

Yes, baker. The memo says the gold and silver articles of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple and carried to Babylon, "…must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God." (Ezra 6:5). That's the order written in the memo. The gold and silver articles are the ones named for the trip home.

The ark is a big name, friend, but it's not in this memo. The memo names "…the gold and silver articles of the house of God…" that Nebuchadnezzar took (Ezra 6:5). Those are the things that must go back to Jerusalem. The text doesn't mention the ark here.

Good thinking about the temple, baker, but the memo doesn't list pillars. It says "…the gold and silver articles of the house of God…" must be returned (Ezra 6:5). Those are what Nebuchadnezzar carried to Babylon. They're the ones headed back to Jerusalem.
That's the one, friend. Darius opens with, "You must stay away from that place!" (Ezra 6:6). No small talk and no warm-up. Tattenai asked questions, and the king answers with a firm hands-off.

That sounds like a king gathering evidence, baker, but it's not what Darius says. His first words to Tattenai are, "You must stay away from that place!" (Ezra 6:6). Nothing in the decree asks for names. Next comes, "Leave this work on the house of God alone." (Ezra 6:7). That's a king saying hands off, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: Stop the work until I come
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Darius doesn't stop anything. He says, "You must stay away from that place!" and then, "Leave this work on the house of God alone." (Ezra 6:6-7). The work keeps going, and the king backs it.

Yes, baker. Darius orders the cost paid in full from the royal treasury "…so that the work will not be hindered." (Ezra 6:8). That order is for the elders who are rebuilding God's house. The point of the money is a work that isn't hindered. I'd bake a lot faster too if somebody covered my flour bill.

Tattenai did the questioning back in Ezra 5, friend, but that's not the word here. Darius says the cost is paid in full "…so that the work will not be hindered." (Ezra 6:8). The point is that the money keeps the work moving.

Inspection is a fair guess, baker, since a king might like to check on his money. But the verse says the cost is paid in full "…so that the work will not be hindered." (Ezra 6:8). The goal is no delays on the building.

That's right, friend. Darius orders the supplies given to them "…as requested by the priests in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 6:9). The verse says they must be given daily without fail. That's a standing order, like a subscription box. The priests are the ones named to do the asking.

The elders are the ones rebuilding, baker, but they're not the ones asking in this verse. The supplies are given daily "…as requested by the priests in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 6:9). The elders do get the building costs covered (Ezra 6:8). The offerings go through the priests.

Prophets show up later in this passage, friend, but not in this verse. Darius orders the supplies given "…as requested by the priests in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 6:9). The priests are the ones making the requests. Haggai and Zechariah, the prophets, come in at Ezra 6:14.

Yes, baker. Darius says the sacrifices let them offer a sweet aroma to the God of heaven "…and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons." (Ezra 6:10). It's right there in the decree. He covers the supplies and asks for prayer too.

Look again, friend. Darius says they will be able to offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven "…and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons." (Ezra 6:10). So the prayer for the king is part of it. The statement was true.

explanations.answer: It becomes a pile of rubble
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Darius says, "…his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense." (Ezra 6:11). It's a serious warning, and that's one heavy part of this passage. Darius wants no one touching that decree.

No handoff to the governor, friend. Darius's warning says, "…his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense." (Ezra 6:11). He's talking about any man who interferes with the directive. The warning names rubble, not a change of owners. This is a heavy part of the passage, so I'll just say it plainly.

A storehouse isn't what the decree names, baker. Darius's warning for any man who interferes says, "…his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense." (Ezra 6:11). The word the king uses is rubble. This is a heavy part of the passage, so I'll leave it at that.

Yes, friend. Darius says, "May God, who has caused His Name to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 6:12). Both altering the decree and destroying the house are covered. He's guarding that house on every side.

Rebellion is what a king usually worries about, baker, but it's not in this line. The words are "…to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 6:12). The focus is on the decree and God's house. Persia isn't mentioned there.

The treasury pays for the work, friend, but robbing it isn't named here. The words are "…to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 6:12). So it's the decree and the house that Darius is guarding.

Yes, baker. The text says Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai and their associates "…diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed." (Ezra 6:13). Diligently is the word the text gives. They did what the king decreed. That's a true statement.

I get why you'd wonder, friend, since Tattenai started out asking questions. But the text says he and his associates "…diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed." (Ezra 6:13). So they did carry it out, and they did it with diligence.

That's it, baker. The elders built and prospered "…through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo." (Ezra 6:14). Two prophets, one building. They had backup from the Lord's own messengers.
Those are big prophet names, friend, but they're not the ones here. The text says "…Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo." (Ezra 6:14). Those two were prophesying while the elders built.

Elijah and Elisha are famous, baker, but they're not named in this verse. The text says the elders built and prospered "…through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo." (Ezra 6:14). Those are the two prophets for this building. Right fame, wrong building site.

Yes, friend. They finished "…according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia." (Ezra 6:14). God's command comes first in the list. The kings' decrees come after it.

The elders are the ones doing the building, baker, but the command doesn't come from them. They finished "…according to the command of the God of Israel…" (Ezra 6:14). The kings' decrees get named right after that.

The priests are in this passage, friend, but the verse puts the command somewhere else. They finished "…according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia." (Ezra 6:14). The command is from the God of Israel.

explanations.answer: The sixth year of King Darius
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The temple was completed on the third day of Adar "…in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius." (Ezra 6:15). The work is done, with every stone and timber in place. That's a finished house.

explanations.answer: The first year of King Cyrus
explanations.explanation: That's the year of the decree, friend, not the finish. Cyrus issued it in his first year (Ezra 6:3). The temple was completed "…in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius." (Ezra 6:15).

Artaxerxes is named in this passage, baker, but not for the finish date. The temple was completed "…in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius." (Ezra 6:15). Artaxerxes only comes up among the kings whose decrees they followed (Ezra 6:14).

explanations.answer: One for each tribe of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The sin offering was "…twelve male goats, one for each tribe of Israel." (Ezra 6:17). It was a sin offering for all Israel. Every tribe is counted.

explanations.answer: One for each month of the year
explanations.explanation: A calendar guess makes sense, baker, since twelve months fits. But the text says the twelve male goats were "…one for each tribe of Israel." (Ezra 6:17). It's a sin offering for all Israel, one goat for every tribe.

explanations.answer: One for each gate of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Gates are a creative guess, friend, but the text goes another way. The twelve male goats were "…one for each tribe of Israel." (Ezra 6:17). That's the reason the verse gives. Nothing about gates comes up here.

Close, baker, but not quite. The priests and Levites were appointed "…according to what is written in the Book of Moses." (Ezra 6:18). Darius's decree covered supplies and money, not the priests' assignments. The order came from the Book of Moses.

Yes, friend. They appointed the priests by their divisions and the Levites by their groups "…according to what is written in the Book of Moses." (Ezra 6:18). So the order for the service followed the Book of Moses. It isn't credited to Darius's decree here. Good catch on a true or false.

That's right, baker. "All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean." (Ezra 6:20). They got ready before the Passover began. Everyone was clean before the lamb was slaughtered.

A fast is a thoughtful guess, friend, but the text doesn't say it. It says "All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean." (Ezra 6:20). Seven days comes up later, but that's for the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Ezra 6:22).

Not this time, baker. The text says "All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean." (Ezra 6:20). Nothing about shaving appears in these verses. The preparation was purification.

Yes, friend. The text says "…the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves." (Ezra 6:20). They did it for everyone, themselves included. That's a big job on a big day.

The elders were busy building, baker, but they aren't named here. The text says "…the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves." (Ezra 6:20). The Levites did the slaughtering.

Haggai and Zechariah are the prophets in this passage, friend, and they come in with the building (Ezra 6:14). But the text gives the slaughtering to others: "…the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves." (Ezra 6:20). So it's the Levites, not the prophets. Right passage, wrong crew.

Not quite, baker. The returned exiles ate it "…together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel." (Ezra 6:21). So others joined the meal too. The table was bigger than just the returnees.

That's right, friend. The Israelites who returned from exile ate it "…together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel." (Ezra 6:21). Those who sought the LORD joined them. It's a bigger table than the statement said.
Yes, baker. They kept the feast with joy "…because the LORD had made them joyful…" (Ezra 6:22). The joy came from the LORD Himself. It's the kind of joy you can't bake yourself, and I've tried.

explanations.answer: Their neighbors made peace with them
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, friend, but the text doesn't say it. They kept the feast with joy "…because the LORD had made them joyful…" (Ezra 6:22). The joy is credited to the LORD, and neighbors don't come into it.
The prophets did prophesy, baker, but that's not the reason given for this joy. The text says "…because the LORD had made them joyful…" (Ezra 6:22). The source is the LORD, not a promise of rest.
